claim: Zona pellucida (ZP) is the extracellular matrix sheltering mammalian oocytes and embryos.
source: Zona pellucida (ZP), the extracellular matrix sheltering mammalian oocytes and embryos, is composed by 3 to 4 proteins.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about ZP that is part of established scientific knowledge in reproductive biology.

claim: Zona pellucida is composed by 3 to 4 proteins.
source: Zona pellucida (ZP), the extracellular matrix sheltering mammalian oocytes and embryos, is composed by 3 to 4 proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ZP composition that is widely accepted in the field.

claim: The roles of the three proteins present in mice have been elucidated by KO models.
source: The roles of the three proteins present in mice have been elucidated by KO models, but the function of the fourth component (ZP4), present in all other eutherian mammals studied so far, has remained elusive.
evidence: This statement references prior research on mouse ZP proteins using knockout models, which is supported by citations in the Introduction section.

claim: ZP4 is present in all other eutherian mammals studied so far (excluding mice).
source: The roles of the three proteins present in mice have been elucidated by KO models, but the function of the fourth component (ZP4), present in all other eutherian mammals studied so far, has remained elusive.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations in the manuscript about ZP4 presence in various mammalian species.

claim: The function of ZP4 has remained elusive.
source: The roles of the three proteins present in mice have been elucidated by KO models, but the function of the fourth component (ZP4), present in all other eutherian mammals studied so far, has remained elusive.
evidence: This statement establishes the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: ZP4 ablation impairs fertility in female rabbits.
source: Herein, we report that ZP4 ablation impairs fertility in female rabbits.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data showing reduced fertility in ZP4 knockout rabbits.

claim: Ovulation is not affected by ZP4 ablation.
source: Ovulation, fertilization and in vitro development to blastocyst were not affected by ZP4 ablation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing ovulation rates between WT, Hz, and KO females.

claim: Fertilization is not affected by ZP4 ablation.
source: Ovulation, fertilization and in vitro development to blastocyst were not affected by ZP4 ablation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on cleavage rates and pronuclei formation.

claim: In vitro development to blastocyst is not affected by ZP4 ablation.
source: Ovulation, fertilization and in vitro development to blastocyst were not affected by ZP4 ablation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing similar blastocyst rates in vitro for WT, Hz, and KO groups.

claim: In vivo development is severely impaired in embryos covered by a ZP4-devoided zona.
source: However, in vivo development is severely impaired in embryos covered by a ZP4-devoided zona, suggesting a defective ZP protective capacity in the absence of ZP4.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced blastocyst rates and developmental arrest in vivo for embryos from ZP4 KO females.

claim: ZP4-devoided zona has defective protective capacity.
source: However, in vivo development is severely impaired in embryos covered by a ZP4-devoided zona, suggesting a defective ZP protective capacity in the absence of ZP4.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that embryos fail to develop properly in vivo but not in vitro, suggesting a protective function is compromised.

claim: ZP4-null ZP is significantly thinner than wild-type ZP.
source: ZP4-null ZP was significantly thinner, more permeable, and exhibited a more disorganized and fenestrated structure.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements of ZP thickness showing approximately 4 µm reduction in KO compared to WT.

claim: ZP4-null ZP is more permeable than wild-type ZP.
source: ZP4-null ZP was significantly thinner, more permeable, and exhibited a more disorganized and fenestrated structure.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that ZP4-null ZP is permeable to 20-40 nm nanospheres while WT ZP blocks them.

claim: ZP4-null ZP exhibits a more disorganized and fenestrated structure.
source: ZP4-null ZP was significantly thinner, more permeable, and exhibited a more disorganized and fenestrated structure.
evidence: This is supported by SEM images showing rougher and more porous texture in ZP4-null ZP compared to WT.

claim: ZP4 is evolutionarily conserved in mammals including humans.
source: The evolutionary conservation of ZP4 in other mammals, including humans, suggests that the structural properties conferred by this protein are required to ensure proper embryo sheltering during in vivo preimplantation development.
evidence: This is supported by citations showing ZP4 presence in multiple mammalian species and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The structural properties conferred by ZP4 are required to ensure proper embryo sheltering during in vivo preimplantation development.
source: The evolutionary conservation of ZP4 in other mammals, including humans, suggests that the structural properties conferred by this protein are required to ensure proper embryo sheltering during in vivo preimplantation development.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing impaired in vivo development and the evolutionary conservation of ZP4.

claim: In eutherian mammals, ZP always contains ZP2 and ZP3 proteins.
source: In all eutherian mammals studied so far ZP always contain ZP2 and ZP3 proteins, but ZP1 or ZP4 may be absent, as both are paralogous genes formed by duplication of a common ancestry gene (reviewed by Goudet et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by a review citation.

claim: ZP1 or ZP4 may be absent in eutherian mammals.
source: In all eutherian mammals studied so far ZP always contain ZP2 and ZP3 proteins, but ZP1 or ZP4 may be absent, as both are paralogous genes formed by duplication of a common ancestry gene (reviewed by Goudet et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a review citation.

claim: ZP1 and ZP4 are paralogous genes formed by duplication of a common ancestry gene.
source: In all eutherian mammals studied so far ZP always contain ZP2 and ZP3 proteins, but ZP1 or ZP4 may be absent, as both are paralogous genes formed by duplication of a common ancestry gene (reviewed by Goudet et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a review citation.

claim: ZP1 serves a structural function in mice.
source: ZP1 serves a structural function, being dispensable for sperm binding or fertilization (Rankin et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research on ZP1 knockout mice.

claim: ZP1 is dispensable for sperm binding or fertilization in mice.
source: ZP1 serves a structural function, being dispensable for sperm binding or fertilization (Rankin et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research on ZP1 knockout mice.

claim: ZP1 null females display perturbed folliculogenesis.
source: ZP1 null females display perturbed folliculogenesis and, although ovulation rates are not affected, both cleavage rate and litter size are reduced, likely due to ZP1-null zona being unable to protect the developing embryo.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research on ZP1 knockout mice.

claim: Ovulation rates are not affected in ZP1 null females.
source: ZP1 null females display perturbed folliculogenesis and, although ovulation rates are not affected, both cleavage rate and litter size are reduced, likely due to ZP1-null zona being unable to protect the developing embryo.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research on ZP1 knockout mice.

claim: Cleavage rate is reduced in ZP1 null females.
source: ZP1 null females display perturbed folliculogenesis and, although ovulation rates are not affected, both cleavage rate and litter size are reduced, likely due to ZP1-null zona being unable to protect the developing embryo.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research on ZP1 knockout mice.

claim: Litter size is reduced in ZP1 null females.
source: ZP1 null females display perturbed folliculogenesis and, although ovulation rates are not affected, both cleavage rate and litter size are reduced, likely due to ZP1-null zona being unable to protect the developing embryo.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research on ZP1 knockout mice.

claim: ZP1-null zona is unable to protect the developing embryo.
source: ZP1 null females display perturbed folliculogenesis and, although ovulation rates are not affected, both cleavage rate and litter size are reduced, likely due to ZP1-null zona being unable to protect the developing embryo.
evidence: This is an inference from prior research cited about ZP1 knockout mice.

claim: ZP2 ablation results in structural defects that are more severe than ZP1 ablation.
source: ZP2 ablation also results in structural defects, which are more severe, as the number of antral follicles is reduced and only few ZP-free oocytes and no two-cell embryos are recovered from Zp2 knock-out (KO) females after mating (Rankin et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research on ZP2 knockout mice.

claim: The number of antral follicles is reduced in Zp2 knockout females.
source: ZP2 ablation also results in structural defects, which are more severe, as the number of antral follicles is reduced and only few ZP-free oocytes and no two-cell embryos are recovered from Zp2 knock-out (KO) females after mating (Rankin et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research on ZP2 knockout mice.

claim: Only few ZP-free oocytes are recovered from Zp2 knockout females after mating.
source: ZP2 ablation also results in structural defects, which are more severe, as the number of antral follicles is reduced and only few ZP-free oocytes and no two-cell embryos are recovered from Zp2 knock-out (KO) females after mating (Rankin et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research on ZP2 knockout mice.

claim: No two-cell embryos are recovered from Zp2 knockout females after mating.
source: ZP2 ablation also results in structural defects, which are more severe, as the number of antral follicles is reduced and only few ZP-free oocytes and no two-cell embryos are recovered from Zp2 knock-out (KO) females after mating (Rankin et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research on ZP2 knockout mice.

claim: Zp3 KO mice are unable to form ZP.
source: Finally, Zp3 KO mice are unable to form ZP, showing a drastic reduction in ovulation rates and also being unable to produce cleaved embryos after mating (Liu et al., 1996; Rankin et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on ZP3 knockout mice.

claim: Zp3 KO mice show a drastic reduction in ovulation rates.
source: Finally, Zp3 KO mice are unable to form ZP, showing a drastic reduction in ovulation rates and also being unable to produce cleaved embryos after mating (Liu et al., 1996; Rankin et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on ZP3 knockout mice.

claim: Zp3 KO mice are unable to produce cleaved embryos after mating.
source: Finally, Zp3 KO mice are unable to form ZP, showing a drastic reduction in ovulation rates and also being unable to produce cleaved embryos after mating (Liu et al., 1996; Rankin et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on ZP3 knockout mice.

claim: ZP2 plays a crucial role in mouse and human sperm recognition.
source: In particular, the generation of ZP composed of different combinations of human ZP proteins (Baibakov et al., 2012) or an heterologous ZP lacking mouse ZP2 protein (Avella et al., 2014) have uncovered a crucial role of ZP2 on mouse and human sperm recognition.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research using transgenic mouse models.

claim: ZP4 is present in humans.
source: The fourth ZP protein component, ZP4, is absent in mice, which seems to be an exception for mammals, as ZP4 is present in multiple mammalian species including humans (Hughes and Barratt, 1999; Lefièvre et al., 2004), rabbits (Stetson et al., 2012), ungulates (Hedrick and Wardrip, 1987; Noguchi et al., 1994; Topper et al., 1997), carnivores (Moros-Nicolás et al., 2018) and other rodents (Hoodbhoy et al., 2005; Izquierdo-Rico et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on ZP4 in various species.

claim: ZP4 is present in rabbits.
source: The fourth ZP protein component, ZP4, is absent in mice, which seems to be an exception for mammals, as ZP4 is present in multiple mammalian species including humans (Hughes and Barratt, 1999; Lefièvre et al., 2004), rabbits (Stetson et al., 2012), ungulates (Hedrick and Wardrip, 1987; Noguchi et al., 1994; Topper et al., 1997), carnivores (Moros-Nicolás et al., 2018) and other rodents (Hoodbhoy et al., 2005; Izquierdo-Rico et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on ZP4 in various species.

claim: ZP4 is present in ungulates.
source: The fourth ZP protein component, ZP4, is absent in mice, which seems to be an exception for mammals, as ZP4 is present in multiple mammalian species including humans (Hughes and Barratt, 1999; Lefièvre et al., 2004), rabbits (Stetson et al., 2012), ungulates (Hedrick and Wardrip, 1987; Noguchi et al., 1994; Topper et al., 1997), carnivores (Moros-Nicolás et al., 2018) and other rodents (Hoodbhoy et al., 2005; Izquierdo-Rico et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on ZP4 in various species.

claim: ZP4 is present in carnivores.
source: The fourth ZP protein component, ZP4, is absent in mice, which seems to be an exception for mammals, as ZP4 is present in multiple mammalian species including humans (Hughes and Barratt, 1999; Lefièvre et al., 2004), rabbits (Stetson et al., 2012), ungulates (Hedrick and Wardrip, 1987; Noguchi et al., 1994; Topper et al., 1997), carnivores (Moros-Nicolás et al., 2018) and other rodents (Hoodbhoy et al., 2005; Izquierdo-Rico et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on ZP4 in various species.

claim: ZP4 is present in other rodents (besides mice).
source: The fourth ZP protein component, ZP4, is absent in mice, which seems to be an exception for mammals, as ZP4 is present in multiple mammalian species including humans (Hughes and Barratt, 1999; Lefièvre et al., 2004), rabbits (Stetson et al., 2012), ungulates (Hedrick and Wardrip, 1987; Noguchi et al., 1994; Topper et al., 1997), carnivores (Moros-Nicolás et al., 2018) and other rodents (Hoodbhoy et al., 2005; Izquierdo-Rico et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on ZP4 in various species.

claim: ZP4 is absent in mice.
source: The fourth ZP protein component, ZP4, is absent in mice, which seems to be an exception for mammals, as ZP4 is present in multiple mammalian species including humans (Hughes and Barratt, 1999; Lefièvre et al., 2004), rabbits (Stetson et al., 2012), ungulates (Hedrick and Wardrip, 1987; Noguchi et al., 1994; Topper et al., 1997), carnivores (Moros-Nicolás et al., 2018) and other rodents (Hoodbhoy et al., 2005; Izquierdo-Rico et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by the absence of ZP4 in mouse ZP studies.

claim: The lack of ZP4 in laboratory mouse has precluded the study of the role of this protein by loss-of-function experiments.
source: The lack of ZP4 in laboratory mouse (Mus musculus), the only species where KO models were readily available, has precluded the study of the role of this protein by of loss-of-function experiments.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the fact that mice lack ZP4 and were the primary model for ZP gene knockout studies.

claim: CRISPR allows direct KO generation in one step.
source: Luckily, the advent of site-specific endonucleases, and particularly CRISPR, the last technology to be developed and the easiest to tailor to its genomic target, allows direct KO generation in one step.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CRISPR technology capabilities.

claim: ZP4-null rabbits were generated using CRISPR technology.
source: Using this technology, we have generated ZP4-null rabbits uncovering that ZP4 confers structural properties to the ZP that are essential to protect the developing preimplantation embryo.
evidence: This is a primary methodological claim supported by the detailed methods and results presented in the manuscript.

claim: ZP4 confers structural properties to the ZP that are essential to protect the developing preimplantation embryo.
source: Using this technology, we have generated ZP4-null rabbits uncovering that ZP4 confers structural properties to the ZP that are essential to protect the developing preimplantation embryo.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data on ZP structure and embryo development.

claim: All 12 pups generated in F0 were edited at the target site.
source: This initial screening revealed that all 12 pups were edited at the target site, but it did not allow to identify each mutated allele harbored by each individual.
evidence: This is supported by experimental genotyping data from the F0 generation.

claim: Mosaicism appears when DNA replication precedes genome edition.
source: This phenomenon appears when DNA replication precedes genome edition and has been commonly observed following zygote microinjection in different mammalian species (Lamas-Toranzo et al., 2017), including rabbits (Guo et al., 2016; Honda et al., 2015; Lv et al., 2016; Song et al., 2016a; Song et al., 2016b; Sui et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2016; Yuan et al., 2016), where genome replication takes place shortly after fertilization (Oprescu et al., 1965; Szollosi, 1966).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations about CRISPR-induced mosaicism.

claim: Genome replication takes place shortly after fertilization in rabbits.
source: This phenomenon appears when DNA replication precedes genome edition and has been commonly observed following zygote microinjection in different mammalian species (Lamas-Toranzo et al., 2017), including rabbits (Guo et al., 2016; Honda et al., 2015; Lv et al., 2016; Song et al., 2016a; Song et al., 2016b; Sui et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2016; Yuan et al., 2016), where genome replication takes place shortly after fertilization (Oprescu et al., 1965; Szollosi, 1966).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations about rabbit embryo development.

claim: None of the seven females generated in F0 were KO.
source: None of the seven females generated in F0 were KO, as all contained at least one in-frame indel (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental genotyping data from the F0 generation.

claim: A non-mosaic male containing two frame-disrupting indels was able to breed normally.
source: A non-mosaic male containing two frame-disrupting indels was able to breed normally, as expected, given that ZP4 protein is exclusively expressed in ovaries.
evidence: This is supported by experimental breeding data and the known ovary-specific expression of ZP4.

claim: ZP4 protein is exclusively expressed in ovaries.
source: A non-mosaic male containing two frame-disrupting indels was able to breed normally, as expected, given that ZP4 protein is exclusively expressed in ovaries.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ZP4 expression pattern.

claim: Protein ablation in KO female individuals was confirmed by IHC in ovaries.
source: Protein ablation in KO female individuals was confirmed by IHC in ovaries (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Proteomics analysis confirmed the absence of ZP4 in KO individuals.
source: Proteomics analysis of solubilized extracts of ZP from oocytes obtained from KO and WT individuals by tandem mass spectrometry further confirmed the absence of ZP4 in KO individuals.
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data from mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: ZP4 ablation did not prevent the synthesis of all other three rabbit ZP proteins (ZP1-3).
source: ZP4 ablation did not prevent the synthesis of all other three rabbit ZP proteins (ZP1-3), which were also detected in the solubilized extract of ZP4 KO ZP (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data showing detection of ZP1-3 in KO samples.

claim: ZP4 ablation does not induce major alterations in ZP1-3 synthesis.
source: This analysis also provides a semi-quantitative estimation of the amount of ZP1-3 proteins based on the number of peptides detected for each protein, which were similar for KO and WT oocytes, thereby suggesting that ZP4 ablation does not induce major alterations in ZP1-3 synthesis.
evidence: This is inferred from proteomics data showing similar peptide counts for ZP1-3 in KO and WT samples.

claim: Only one out of 10 KO females delivered a single litter of reduced size (four pups).
source: WT and Hz females delivered normal litter sizes, whereas only one out of 10 KO females, delivered a single litter of reduced size (four pups, Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental fertility data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: WT and Hz females delivered normal litter sizes.
source: WT and Hz females delivered normal litter sizes, whereas only one out of 10 KO females, delivered a single litter of reduced size (four pups, Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental fertility data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Ovulation rates following natural mating were similar between WT, Hz, and KO groups.
source: Ovulation rates following natural mating were similar between all groups, suggesting that ZP4 ablation did not impair folliculogenesis (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on ovulation rates shown in Figure 2B.

claim: ZP4 ablation did not impair folliculogenesis.
source: Ovulation rates following natural mating were similar between all groups, suggesting that ZP4 ablation did not impair folliculogenesis (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ovulation rates were similar across groups.

claim: ZP4 disrupted ovaries were grossly indistinguishable from WT or Hz ovaries.
source: ZP4 disrupted ovaries were grossly indistinguishable from WT or Hz and no obvious abnormalities were noted in follicular population (Figure 2E–H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis data shown in Figure 2 and supplementary figures.

claim: No obvious abnormalities were noted in follicular population in ZP4 KO ovaries.
source: ZP4 disrupted ovaries were grossly indistinguishable from WT or Hz and no obvious abnormalities were noted in follicular population (Figure 2E–H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis data shown in Figure 2 and supplementary figures.

claim: Cleavage rates did not differ between WT, Hz, and KO groups.
source: Cleavage rates did not differ between the different groups, suggesting that ZP4 does not play an essential role in fertilization in vivo (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on cleavage rates shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ZP4 does not play an essential role in fertilization in vivo.
source: Cleavage rates did not differ between the different groups, suggesting that ZP4 does not play an essential role in fertilization in vivo (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cleavage rates were similar across groups.

claim: No differences were noted in blastocyst rates between WT, Hz, and KO groups in vitro.
source: Again, no differences were noted in blastocyst rates or morphology, showing that embryos derived from ZP4-null oocytes (Hz embryos enclosed by a ZP4-null ZP, MATKO embryos) are able to reach the blastocyst stage in vitro (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on blastocyst rates shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Embryos derived from ZP4-null oocytes are able to reach the blastocyst stage in vitro.
source: Again, no differences were noted in blastocyst rates or morphology, showing that embryos derived from ZP4-null oocytes (Hz embryos enclosed by a ZP4-null ZP, MATKO embryos) are able to reach the blastocyst stage in vitro (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on blastocyst development shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Normal pronuclear formation was noted for embryos derived from ZP4-null oocytes.
source: Normal pronuclear formation was noted for embryos derived from ZP4-null oocytes, showing no effect of ZP4 ablation on the in vivo fertilization process (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on pronuclei formation shown in Figure 2G.

claim: ZP4 ablation has no effect on the in vivo fertilization process.
source: Normal pronuclear formation was noted for embryos derived from ZP4-null oocytes, showing no effect of ZP4 ablation on the in vivo fertilization process (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of normal pronuclei formation in ZP4-null embryos.

claim: Rabbit ZP is not involved in polyspermy blockage.
source: As expected, given that rabbit ZP is not involved in polyspermy blockage (Pincus and Enzmann, 1932), no polyspermy was found on embryos produced from ZP4-null oocytes.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation about rabbit ZP function.

claim: No polyspermy was found on embryos produced from ZP4-null oocytes.
source: As expected, given that rabbit ZP is not involved in polyspermy blockage (Pincus and Enzmann, 1932), no polyspermy was found on embryos produced from ZP4-null oocytes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations of embryos from ZP4-null oocytes.

claim: The negative effect of ZP4 ablation can only be attributed to a developmental failure of the embryos surrounded by a ZP lacking ZP4.
source: As ovulation and fertilization were not affected in ZP4-null females, the negative effect of ZP4 ablation can only be attributed to a developmental failure of the embryos surrounded by a ZP lacking ZP4.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ovulation and fertilization were normal but fertility was impaired.

claim: The developmental failure of ZP4-null embryos must occur in vivo.
source: However, given that these Hz embryos derived from ZP4-disrupted oocytes were able to develop in vitro to the blastocyst stage, this developmental failure must occur in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that embryos develop normally in vitro but not in vivo.

claim: Rabbit embryos without zona are unable to establish pregnancy following embryo transfer.
source: ZP protection is essential for in vivo embryo development, as rabbit embryos without zona are unable to establish pregnancy following embryo transfer (Moore et al., 1968; Rottmann and Lampeter, 1981).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations about zona-free rabbit embryos.

claim: Rabbit embryos have developed to the blastocyst stage and are surrounded by a mucin coat by Day 4 post-mating.
source: At this developmental time, rabbit embryos have developed to the blastocyst stage and are surrounded by a mucin coat, but lack ZP, which disappears between Days 3 and 4 (Denker and Gerdes, 1979; Fischer et al., 1991).
evidence: This is established knowledge about rabbit embryo development supported by citations.

claim: Rabbit ZP disappears between Days 3 and 4 post-mating.
source: At this developmental time, rabbit embryos have developed to the blastocyst stage and are surrounded by a mucin coat, but lack ZP, which disappears between Days 3 and 4 (Denker and Gerdes, 1979; Fischer et al., 1991).
evidence: This is established knowledge about rabbit embryo development supported by citations.

claim: ZP dissolution does not occur in vitro as it requires both embryo development and uterine secretions.
source: ZP dissolution does not occur in vitro as it requires both from embryo development and uterine secretions (Fischer et al., 1991).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation about ZP dissolution requirements.

claim: All embryos recovered from WT females at Day 4 post-mating had reached the blastocyst stage.
source: All embryos recovered from WT females at Day 4 post-mating had reached the blastocyst stage, however, less than half of the MATKO embryos recovered from KO females were able to develop to the blastocyst stage (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on Day 4 embryo development shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Less than half of the MATKO embryos recovered from KO females were able to develop to the blastocyst stage by Day 4.
source: All embryos recovered from WT females at Day 4 post-mating had reached the blastocyst stage, however, less than half of the MATKO embryos recovered from KO females were able to develop to the blastocyst stage (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on Day 4 embryo development shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Blastocysts from KO females showed a significant reduction in blastocyst expansion compared to WT (~500 vs. ~200 µm diameter).
source: Moreover, those embryos reaching the blastocyst stage in the KO group showed a significant reduction in blastocyst expansion (~500 vs.~200 µm diameter for WT vs. KO, respectively, Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements of blastocyst diameter shown in Figure 3B.

claim: ZP was absent in all WT blastocysts at Day 4.
source: ZP was absent in all WT blastocysts (Figure 3C) and in most expanded or collapsed blastocysts from the KO group, but was present in all degenerated embryos (Figure 3D), in agreement with the requirement of embryo development for ZP dissolution previously reported (Fischer et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ZP was present in all degenerated embryos from the KO group at Day 4.
source: ZP was absent in all WT blastocysts (Figure 3C) and in most expanded or collapsed blastocysts from the KO group, but was present in all degenerated embryos (Figure 3D), in agreement with the requirement of embryo development for ZP dissolution previously reported (Fischer et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Embryo development is required for ZP dissolution.
source: ZP was absent in all WT blastocysts (Figure 3C) and in most expanded or collapsed blastocysts from the KO group, but was present in all degenerated embryos (Figure 3D), in agreement with the requirement of embryo development for ZP dissolution previously reported (Fischer et al., 1991).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation and confirmed by experimental observations.

claim: Evident signs of mechanical damage could be observed in degenerated embryos in the KO group.
source: Evident signs of mechanical damage (non-spherical, crushed ZP) could be observed in degenerated embryos in the KO group (Figure 3D), suggesting that mechanical pressure may be at least partially responsible for the developmental failure.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Mechanical pressure may be at least partially responsible for the developmental failure in ZP4-null embryos.
source: Evident signs of mechanical damage (non-spherical, crushed ZP) could be observed in degenerated embryos in the KO group (Figure 3D), suggesting that mechanical pressure may be at least partially responsible for the developmental failure.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of mechanical damage in degenerated embryos.

claim: Rabbit embryo undergoes relevant embryonic growth between Day 4 and Day 6 before implantation.
source: Beyond Day 4 and before implantation, the rabbit embryo undergo a relevant embryonic growth that has not been recapitulated yet on an in vitro setting.
evidence: This is established knowledge about rabbit embryo development.

claim: Rabbit embryo growth from Days 4 to 6 converts a ~500 µm blastocyst to a ~3 mm expanded blastocyst.
source: This growth, converting a ~ 500 µm blastocyst to a ~ 3 mm expanded blastocysts from Days 4 to 6, is concomitant to the formation of a new glycoprotein matrix termed neozona and the replacement of the mucin coat by the gloiolemma (Fischer et al., 1991).
evidence: This is established knowledge about rabbit embryo development supported by a citation.

claim: Formation of neozona occurs between Days 4 to 6 in rabbit embryos.
source: This growth, converting a ~ 500 µm blastocyst to a ~ 3 mm expanded blastocysts from Days 4 to 6, is concomitant to the formation of a new glycoprotein matrix termed neozona and the replacement of the mucin coat by the gloiolemma (Fischer et al., 1991).
evidence: This is established knowledge about rabbit embryo development supported by a citation.

claim: The mucin coat is replaced by the gloiolemma between Days 4 to 6 in rabbit embryos.
source: This growth, converting a ~ 500 µm blastocyst to a ~ 3 mm expanded blastocysts from Days 4 to 6, is concomitant to the formation of a new glycoprotein matrix termed neozona and the replacement of the mucin coat by the gloiolemma (Fischer et al., 1991).
evidence: This is established knowledge about rabbit embryo development supported by a citation.

claim: More than half of the MATKO embryos had been lost by Day 6 after mating.

claim: ZP lacking ZP4 appeared thinner and more irregular (less spherical) compared to WT ZP.

claim: ZP4-null ZP showed a significant reduction (~4 µm) in thickness compared to WT ZP.

claim: No differences in ZP thickness were noticed between WT or Hz females.

claim: ZP4 does not play an essential role during the fertilization process in vivo.
source: Although we cannot assure that ZP4 ablation might reduce sperm binding, acrosome reaction or sperm penetration in vitro, our results unequivocally show that ZP4 does not play an essential role during the fertilization process in vivo, but serves a structural and mechanical function which is fundamental to protect the developing embryo prior to implantation.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data showing normal fertilization in ZP4 KO females.

claim: ZP4 serves a structural and mechanical function which is fundamental to protect the developing embryo prior to implantation.

evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data on ZP structure and embryo development.

claim: ZP plays an essential protective role during preimplantation embryo development.

evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations about zona-free embryo development.
